claim: Chemosensation of phenazines produced by pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa leads to rapid activation of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ neurons.
source: Here we show that chemosensation of phenazines produced by pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which leads to rapid activation of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ neurons, is insufficient for the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Meisel et al., 2014) and is part of the manuscript's findings.

claim: Chemosensation of phenazines produced by pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa is insufficient for the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior.
source: Here we show that chemosensation of phenazines produced by pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which leads to rapid activation of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ neurons, is insufficient for the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa.
source: Instead, intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulates both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating not only the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway but also the G-protein coupled receptor NPR-1 pathway, which also controls aerotaxis behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, demonstrating correlation between virulence and bloating/avoidance.

claim: Intestinal infection and bloating regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway.
source: Instead, intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulates both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating not only the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway but also the G-protein coupled receptor NPR-1 pathway, which also controls aerotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: Intestinal infection and bloating regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the NPR-1 pathway.
source: Instead, intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulates both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating not only the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway but also the G-protein coupled receptor NPR-1 pathway, which also controls aerotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: The NPR-1 pathway controls aerotaxis behavior.
source: Instead, intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulates both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating not only the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway but also the G-protein coupled receptor NPR-1 pathway, which also controls aerotaxis behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Chang et al., 2006; de Bono et al., 2002) and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Modulation of neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection serves as a systemic feedback that enables animals to avoid virulent bacteria.
source: Modulation of these neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection serves as a systemic feedback that enables animals to avoid virulent bacteria.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Feedback from the intestine during infection can modulate the behavior, learning, and microbial perception of the host.
source: These results reveal how feedback from the intestine during infection can modulate the behavior, learning, and microbial perception of the host.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Physical avoidance of pathogens is a critical defense strategy to reduce pathogen infections.
source: Physical avoidance of pathogens is also a critical defense strategy to reduce pathogen infections (Kavaliers et al., 2019; Medzhitov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chemosensation of bacterial metabolites and toxins plays an important role in eliciting pathogen avoidance behaviors.
source: Chemosensation of bacterial metabolites and toxins appears to play an important role in eliciting pathogen avoidance behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in mammals and Drosophila.

claim: In mammals, olfactory chemosensory neurons and nociceptor sensory neurons detect bacterial toxins, quorum-sensing molecules, formyl peptides, and lipopolysaccharides through distinct molecular mechanisms that lead to rapid avoidance behaviors.
source: In mammals, olfactory chemosensory neurons and nociceptor sensory neurons detect bacterial toxins, quorum-sensing molecules, formyl peptides, and lipopolysaccharides through distinct molecular mechanisms that lead to rapid avoidance behaviors (Boillat et al., 2015; Chiu et al., 2013; Meseguer et al., 2014; Rivière et al., 2009; Tizzano et al., 2010; Yang and Chiu, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, olfactory and gustatory neurons detect geosmin, phenol, and lipopolysaccharides via distinct molecular mechanisms, allowing the organism to avoid food contaminated with bacteria.
source: Similarly, in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, olfactory and gustatory neurons have been reported to detect geosmin (the smell of mold), phenol, and lipopolysaccharides via distinct molecular mechanisms, allowing the organism to avoid food contaminated with bacteria (Mansourian et al., 2016; Soldano et al., 2016; Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pathogenic bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa infect and kill C. elegans.
source: Pathogenic bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa infect and kill C. elegans, and upon exposure to P. aeruginosa, C. elegans elicits an innate immune response that results in the activation of microbial-killing pathways and a pathogen-avoidance behavior that improve its survival (Martin et al., 2017; Meisel and Kim, 2014; Styer et al., 2008; Troemel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon exposure to P. aeruginosa, C. elegans elicits an innate immune response that results in the activation of microbial-killing pathways and a pathogen-avoidance behavior that improve its survival.
source: Pathogenic bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa infect and kill C. elegans, and upon exposure to P. aeruginosa, C. elegans elicits an innate immune response that results in the activation of microbial-killing pathways and a pathogen-avoidance behavior that improve its survival (Martin et al., 2017; Meisel and Kim, 2014; Styer et al., 2008; Troemel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chemosensation of the P. aeruginosa metabolites phenazine-1-carboxamide and pyochelin has been proposed to be responsible for eliciting the avoidance behavior.
source: Chemosensation of the P. aeruginosa metabolites phenazine-1-carboxamide and pyochelin has been proposed to be responsible for eliciting the avoidance behavior (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: P. aeruginosa metabolites activate a G-protein signaling pathway in the ASJ chemosensory neuron pair that induces expression of the neuromodulator DAF-7/TGF-β within minutes of exposure to the pathogen.
source: These metabolites activate a G-protein signaling pathway in the ASJ chemosensory neuron pair that induces expression of the neuromodulator DAF-7/TGF-β within minutes of exposure to the pathogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Meisel et al., 2014).

claim: C. elegans are initially attracted towards lawns of P. aeruginosa and only begin to avoid the pathogen after exposure for hours.
source: However, the animals are initially attracted towards lawns of P. aeruginosa and only begin to avoid the pathogen after exposure for hours (Meisel et al., 2014; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The initial attraction of C. elegans towards P. aeruginosa is mediated by sensing of quorum-sensing molecules acylated homoserine lactones.
source: The initial attraction of C. elegans towards P. aeruginosa is mediated by sensing of quorum-sensing molecules acylated homoserine lactones (Beale et al., 2006; Ha et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In a two-choice preference assay between Escherichia coli and P. aeruginosa, naïve animals show a higher preference for P. aeruginosa.
source: In addition, in a two-choice preference assay between Escherichia coli and P. aeruginosa, the naïve animals show a higher preference for P. aeruginosa (Ha et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Animals change their choice and move towards E. coli lawns after an exposure time to the two bacteria exceeding 4 hr.
source: The animals only change their choice and move towards E. coli lawns after an exposure time to the two bacteria exceeding 4 hr (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The activation of DAF-7/TGF-β signaling in ASJ neurons does not fully explain the later aversive learning towards P. aeruginosa.
source: Thus, the activation of DAF-7/TGF-β signaling in ASJ neurons, which takes place after minutes of exposure to P. aeruginosa, does not fully explain the later aversive learning towards P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing mismatch between DAF-7 activation (minutes) and avoidance behavior (hours).

claim: Bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by the pathogen infection underlies the avoidance behavior via modulation of both DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathways.
source: Here we show that chemosensation of P. aeruginosa metabolites, which leads to the induction of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ neurons, does not correlate with the avoidance behavior. Instead, bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by the pathogen infection underlies the avoidance behavior via modulation of both DAF-7/TGF-β and the G-protein coupled receptor NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathways, which regulate aerotaxis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 3-6.

claim: Modulation of neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection drives the change in preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns.
source: We further show that the modulation of these neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection or genetic modulation of aerotaxis by loss of ocr-2 and osm-9 drives the change in preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Genetic modulation of aerotaxis by loss of ocr-2 and osm-9 drives the change in preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns.
source: We further show that the modulation of these neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection or genetic modulation of aerotaxis by loss of ocr-2 and osm-9 drives the change in preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Signaling from the intestine via neuroendocrine pathways modulates microbial perception during infection.
source: Our findings demonstrate that signaling from the intestine via neuroendocrine pathways modulates microbial perception during infection.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: P. aeruginosa uses a well-characterized biosynthetic pathway to generate four different phenazines.
source: P. aeruginosa uses a well-characterized biosynthetic pathway to generate four different phenazines (Dietrich et al., 2006) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid is the precursor of all other phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa.
source: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid, the precursor of all other phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa, is synthesized from chorismate by a full set of functional phenazine-1-carboxylic acid biosynthetic enzymes encoded by the phzA1-G1 and phzA2-G2 operons (Dietrich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid is synthesized from chorismate by enzymes encoded by the phzA1-G1 and phzA2-G2 operons.
source: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid, the precursor of all other phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa, is synthesized from chorismate by a full set of functional phenazine-1-carboxylic acid biosynthetic enzymes encoded by the phzA1-G1 and phzA2-G2 operons (Dietrich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid can be modified by other enzymes to make 1-hydroxyphenazine, phenazine-1-carboxamide, or pyocyanin.
source: Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid can be modified by other enzymes to make 1-hydroxyphenazine, phenazine-1-carboxamide, or pyocyanin (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1A and is based on established knowledge of phenazine biosynthesis.

claim: Phenazine-1-carboxamide, but not other phenazines, activates DAF-7/TGF-β expression in ASJ neurons.
source: Phenazine-1-carboxamide, but not other phenazines, activates DAF-7/TGF-β expression in ASJ neurons (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Animals exposed to E. coli lawns containing phenazine-1-carboxamide did not exhibit the avoidance behavior.
source: We found that animals exposed to E. coli lawns containing phenazine-1-carboxamide, which is required for the activation of DAF-7/TGF-β expression in ASJ neurons (Meisel et al., 2014), did not exhibit the avoidance behavior (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Animals did not avoid E. coli lawns with added phenazine-1-carboxylic acid and pyocyanin.
source: Additionally, the animals did not avoid E. coli lawns with added phenazine-1-carboxylic acid and pyocyanin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Animals did avoid lawns of E. coli containing 1-hydroxyphenazine.
source: In contrast, the animals did avoid lawns of E. coli containing 1-hydroxyphenazine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Animals feeding on E. coli lawns supplemented with 1-hydroxyphenazine showed bloating of the intestinal lumen.
source: We observed that animals feeding on E. coli lawns that were supplemented with 1-hydroxyphenazine, but not other phenazines, showed bloating of the intestinal lumen (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Bloating of the intestine elicits microbial avoidance behavior, including the avoidance of E. coli.
source: Bloating of the intestine is known to elicit microbial avoidance behavior, including the avoidance of E. coli (Kumar et al., 2019; Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The avoidance of E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine was likely caused by intestinal bloating of the animals induced by the toxin.
source: Therefore, the avoidance of E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine was likely caused by intestinal bloating of the animals induced by the toxin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between 1-hydroxyphenazine exposure, intestinal bloating, and avoidance behavior.

claim: Animals feeding on E. coli lawns supplemented with 1-hydroxyphenazine showed drastically reduced survival.
source: We also observed that animals feeding on E. coli lawns supplemented with 1-hydroxyphenazine, but not other phenazines, showed drastically reduced survival (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: More than 50% of the animals feeding on E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine died within 24 hr.
source: More than 50% of the animals feeding on E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine died within 24 hr, while animals feeding on control E. coli lawns or E. coli lawns containing other phenazines remained alive at the same time point (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: However, P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1G), suggesting that the addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
source: However, P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1G), suggesting that the addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phenazine mutants are not attenuated in killing, yet exogenous 1-hydroxyphenazine is highly toxic.

claim: All the phenazine mutants induced an avoidance behavior that was indistinguishable from that caused by the wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: Moreover, all the phenazine mutants induced an avoidance behavior that was indistinguishable from that caused by the wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The normal amount of phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa during infection is insufficient for induction of the avoidance behavior.
source: These results suggest that while high amounts of externally added 1-hydroxyphenazine elicit microbial avoidance behavior, the normal amount of phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa during infection is insufficient for induction of the avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that phenazine mutants still induce avoidance.

claim: The initial phase of interaction before elicitation of the avoidance behavior is variable, leading to different avoidance kinetics in various studies.
source: However, the initial phase of interaction before elicitation of the avoidance behavior is variable, leading to different avoidance kinetics in various studies (Hao et al., 2018; Hilbert and Kim, 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Meisel et al., 2014; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies showing variability.

claim: Variations in avoidance kinetics are likely due to differences in the production of P. aeruginosa factors governing the avoidance behavior.
source: It is likely that the variations in avoidance kinetics are due to differences in the production of P. aeruginosa factors governing the avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain observed variability.

claim: Different growing conditions for the P. aeruginosa lawns might be responsible for the differences in avoidance behaviors.
source: We reasoned that different growing conditions for the P. aeruginosa lawns might be responsible for the differences in avoidance behaviors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: One of the major differences in bacterial lawn preparations is the variation in incubation periods of P. aeruginosa on agar plates before animal exposure.
source: We observed that one of the major differences in bacterial lawn preparations is the variation in incubation periods of P. aeruginosa on agar plates before animal exposure (Hao et al., 2018; Hilbert and Kim, 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Meisel et al., 2014; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of methods in cited studies.

claim: The avoidance behavior of the animals was enhanced with the incubation period of the P. aeruginosa lawns.
source: The avoidance behavior of the animals was enhanced with the incubation period of the P. aeruginosa lawns (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns incubated at 37°C for 24 hr followed by 25°C for 48 hr showed a significantly enhanced avoidance rate compared to animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns incubated at 37°C for 12 hr.
source: Animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns that were incubated at 37°C for 24 hr followed by 25°C for 48 hr (referred to as 72 hr lawn) showed a significantly enhanced avoidance rate in comparison to animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns that were incubated at 37°C for 12 hr (referred to as 12 hr lawn) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns.
source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2D,E), animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns.
source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2D,E), animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons was not significantly different in animals exposed to 12 or 72 hr lawns.
source: In addition, the induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons was not significantly different in animals exposed to 12 or 72 hr lawns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ may not be the only cause of the elicitation of avoidance behavior.
source: Because the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons was indistinguishable in animals on 12 and 72 hr lawns, the results suggest that the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ may not be the only cause of the elicitation of avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that daf-7 induction is similar but avoidance kinetics differ.

claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr.
source: We found that animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr, while the lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: The lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli.
source: We found that animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr, while the lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: Bloating of the intestine leads to the induction of genes that are part of the NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathway.
source: Because bloating of the intestine leads to the induction of genes that are part of the NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathway (Singh and Aballay, 2019a), we examined the expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns, but not to 12 hr lawns, showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns did not show higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns, but not to 12 hr lawns, showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of nol-6 reduces bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by bacterial infection.
source: Previous studies have shown that RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated knockdown of nol-6, a nucleolar RNA-associated protein, reduces bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by bacterial infection (Fuhrman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: nol-6 RNAi delayed pathogen avoidance.
source: We found that nol-6 RNAi delayed pathogen avoidance (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Animals deficient in nol-6 failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr.
source: Animals deficient in nol-6, which failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr (Figure 3E), did not exhibit intestinal bloating at the same time point when exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: Animals deficient in nol-6 did not exhibit intestinal bloating at 8 hr when exposed to 72 hr lawns.
source: Animals deficient in nol-6, which failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr (Figure 3E), did not exhibit intestinal bloating at the same time point when exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr.
source: Consistent with the idea that bloating induces pathogen avoidance, nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr (Figure 3E), at which time they also exhibited intestinal bloating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: nol-6 RNAi animals exhibited intestinal bloating at 24 hr when exposed to 72 hr lawns.
source: Consistent with the idea that bloating induces pathogen avoidance, nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr (Figure 3E), at which time they also exhibited intestinal bloating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior.
source: These results indicate that nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior, and the delayed avoidance behavior is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nol-6 RNAi animals eventually avoid P. aeruginosa when bloating occurs.

claim: The delayed avoidance behavior in nol-6 RNAi animals is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
source: These results indicate that nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior, and the delayed avoidance behavior is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between delayed bloating and delayed avoidance in nol-6 RNAi animals.

claim: Knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons.
source: Despite diminishing the avoidance behavior, knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in either ASJ (Figure 3H) or ASI neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons.
source: Despite diminishing the avoidance behavior, knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in either ASJ (Figure 3H) or ASI neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Bloating of the intestine, but not induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, underlies the avoidance behavior.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that bloating of the intestine, but not induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, underlies the avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that bloating correlates with avoidance while daf-7 induction does not.

claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization.
source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure.
source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intestinal bloating on 72 hr lawns is independent of bacterial colonization.
source: These results indicate that intestinal bloating on 72 hr lawns is independent of bacterial colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that bloating occurs without increased colonization on 72 hr lawns.

claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns.
source: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns (Figure 4B), indicating that the virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
source: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns (Figure 4B), indicating that the virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival data showing faster death on 72 hr lawns.

claim: A non-virulent P. aeruginosa strain deficient in the gene gacA fails to elicit C. elegans avoidance.
source: It has been shown that a non-virulent P. aeruginosa strain deficient in the gene gacA, a global activator of gene expression and virulence, fails to elicit C. elegans avoidance (Hao et al., 2018; Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: P. aeruginosa gacA mutants are hampered in the induction of daf-7 in the ASJ chemosensory neuron.
source: P. aeruginosa gacA mutants are also hampered in the induction of daf-7 in the ASJ chemosensory neuron (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All studied P. aeruginosa mutants exhibited reduced virulence compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: We confirmed that all the studied P. aeruginosa mutants exhibited reduced virulence compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All studied P. aeruginosa mutants were deficient in the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior.
source: All of these mutants were also deficient in the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons.
source: We found that while kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, the induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: We found that while kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, the induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons by all studied P. aeruginosa mutants was indistinguishable from the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons by all of these P. aeruginosa mutants was indistinguishable from the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of daf-7 induction in the ASJ neurons induced by different P. aeruginosa mutants did not show any correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns.
source: The levels of daf-7 induction in the ASJ neurons induced by different P. aeruginosa mutants did not show any correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The mean survival of the animals on different P. aeruginosa mutants showed a strong correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns.
source: In contrast, the mean survival of the animals on different P. aeruginosa mutants showed a strong correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The virulence of P. aeruginosa, and not its ability to induce daf-7 in ASJ neurons, correlates with C. elegans avoidance behavior.
source: Taken together, these results show that the virulence of P. aeruginosa, and not its ability to induce daf-7 in ASJ neurons, correlates with C. elegans avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing correlation between virulence and avoidance but not between daf-7 induction and avoidance.

claim: Prior exposure to P. aeruginosa for several hours enables C. elegans to preferentially choose nonpathogenic E. coli over P. aeruginosa.
source: It is known that prior exposure to P. aeruginosa for several hours enables C. elegans to preferentially choose nonpathogenic E. coli over P. aeruginosa (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: When naïve animals were given a choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa, the animals changed their preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli after 8 hr of exposure.
source: Similarly, in a two-choice assay, when naïve animals were given a choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa, the animals changed their preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli after 8 hr of exposure (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Aerotaxis plays a role in pathogen avoidance.
source: Because aerotaxis plays a role in pathogen avoidance (Meisel et al., 2014; Reddy et al., 2009; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Styer et al., 2008), we examined whether aerotaxis is also important for changes in preference from pathogenic to nonpathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: P. aeruginosa lawns have lower oxygen levels than E. coli lawns.
source: It is known that P. aeruginosa lawns have lower oxygen levels than E. coli lawns (Gray et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of the gene cysl-2 is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1).
source: Expression of the gene cysl-2 is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), a transcription factor that is induced by low levels of oxygen (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels.
source: Since HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels (Jiang et al., 2001), the expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
source: Since HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels (Jiang et al., 2001), the expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known regulation of HIF-1 by oxygen levels.

claim: Animals exposed for 24 hr to P. aeruginosa lawns had higher GFP levels compared with those exposed to E. coli lawns.
source: We found that animals exposed for 24 hr to P. aeruginosa lawns had higher GFP levels compared with those exposed to E. coli lawns (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1 inhibited pathogen avoidance.
source: We observed that the loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1, which are deficient in DAF-7/TGF-β, and NPR-1 signaling, respectively, inhibited both pathogen avoidance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1 inhibited the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli.
source: We observed that the loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1, which are deficient in DAF-7/TGF-β, and NPR-1 signaling, respectively, inhibited both pathogen avoidance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1 signaling pathways act in parallel.
source: These two neuroendocrine pathways are known to act in parallel (Chang et al., 2006; de Bono et al., 2002); therefore, we investigated the behaviors of daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phenotypes of pathogen avoidance and change in preference were enhanced in daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals.
source: We found that the aforementioned phenotypes were enhanced in daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aerotaxis-regulating pathways are required for the change in microbial preference upon pathogen infection.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that aerotaxis-regulating pathways are required for the change in microbial preference upon pathogen infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that mutations in aerotaxis pathways prevent preference changes.

claim: The increased preference for low oxygen in loss of function npr-1 and daf-7 mutants requires the function of the TRPV genes osm-9 and ocr-2.
source: The increased preference for low oxygen in loss of function npr-1 and daf-7 mutants requires the function of the transient receptor potential channel vanilloid (TRPV) genes osm-9 and ocr-2 (Chang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of function ocr-2 and osm-9 mutants have an increased preference for high oxygen levels.
source: Because loss of function ocr-2 and osm-9 mutants have an increased preference for high oxygen levels (Chang et al., 2006), and because E. coli lawns have relatively higher oxygen levels (Gray et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2011), we reasoned that these mutants should rapidly change their preference to E. coli if given the choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals exhibited a strong enhancement of avoidance behavior.
source: As expected, ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals exhibited a strong enhancement of avoidance behavior (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals showed a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
source: These animals also showed a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The preference for high oxygen in ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) mutants is suppressed by the loss of function mutation in egl-9.
source: The preference for high oxygen in ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) mutants is suppressed by the loss of function mutation in egl-9, a negative regulator of HIF-1 (Chang and Bargmann, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The egl-9 mutation suppressed both the enhanced pathogen avoidance and E. coli preference of osm-9(yz6) animals.
source: Consistent with the function of EGL-9, we observed that the egl-9 mutation suppressed both the enhanced pathogen avoidance and E. coli preference of osm-9(yz6) animals (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Aerotaxis regulates both P. aeruginosa avoidance and changes in microbial preference.
source: These results show that aerotaxis regulates both P. aeruginosa avoidance and changes in microbial preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that genetic manipulation of aerotaxis affects both avoidance and preference.

claim: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways.
source: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways, which results in a preference towards high oxygen (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection results in a preference towards high oxygen.
source: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways, which results in a preference towards high oxygen (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Knockdown of aex-5 and egl-8 caused bloating of the intestinal lumen and led to enhanced avoidance of P. aeruginosa.
source: Knockdown of these genes caused bloating of the intestinal lumen and led to enhanced avoidance of P. aeruginosa (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of aex-5 and egl-8 by RNAi and mutations elicited a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
source: As shown in Figure 6E,F, inhibition of these genes by RNAi and mutations also elicited a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: Exposure to 5% oxygen elicited a rapid preference towards E. coli.
source: We were also able to elicit a rapid preference towards E. coli by exposing the animals to 5% oxygen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to low oxygen levels alone does not affect either intestinal bacterial colonization or bloating.
source: Exposure to low oxygen levels alone does not affect either intestinal bacterial colonization or bloating (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: nol-6 RNAi animals are resistant to P. aeruginosa infection and bloating.
source: We studied the change in microbial preference in nol-6 RNAi animals that are resistant to P. aeruginosa infection and bloating.
evidence: This is based on prior characterization of nol-6 RNAi animals and data shown earlier in the manuscript.

claim: nol-6 RNAi animals were defective in aversive learning toward P. aeruginosa.
source: As shown in Figure 6G, nol-6 RNAi animals were defective in aversive learning toward P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Intestinal bloating caused by pathogen infection is important for the learning process that leads to change in microbial preference from bacterial lawns containing relatively lower to those containing relatively higher oxygen levels.
source: Together, these results suggest that intestinal bloating caused by pathogen infection, which modulates aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways, is important for the learning process that leads to change in microbial preference from bacterial lawns containing relatively lower to those containing relatively higher oxygen levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the neuroendocrine pathways NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β that control aerotaxis behavior.
source: Our study establishes that intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the neuroendocrine pathways NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β that control aerotaxis behavior (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Enhanced activities of NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways lead to the avoidance of low oxygen.
source: Enhanced activities of these pathways, as a consequence of intestinal infection, lead to the avoidance of low oxygen, resulting in the avoidance of bacterial lawns with low oxygen due to microbial metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Enhanced activities of NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways result in the avoidance of bacterial lawns with low oxygen due to microbial metabolism.
source: Enhanced activities of these pathways, as a consequence of intestinal infection, lead to the avoidance of low oxygen, resulting in the avoidance of bacterial lawns with low oxygen due to microbial metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Intestinal infection-mediated avoidance of low oxygen drives the movement of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns.
source: Intestinal infection-mediated avoidance of low oxygen also drives the movement of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns, which have been reported to have relatively higher oxygen levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Modulation of aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection plays a role in the learning process, resulting in changes in the preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli.
source: Thus, modulation of aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal infection plays a role in the learning process, resulting in changes in the preference of animals from P. aeruginosa to E. coli (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Microbial perception is controlled by inputs from the intestine during infection in C. elegans.
source: Our study also indicates that microbial perception is controlled by inputs from the intestine during infection in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The induction of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ chemosensory neurons was observed within 6 min of exposure to P. aeruginosa.
source: The induction of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ chemosensory neurons was observed within 6 min of exposure to P. aeruginosa, and no further changes were observed up to 24 hr (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: No further changes in DAF-7/TGF-β induction in ASJ neurons were observed up to 24 hr after initial exposure to P. aeruginosa.
source: The induction of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ chemosensory neurons was observed within 6 min of exposure to P. aeruginosa, and no further changes were observed up to 24 hr (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The avoidance behavior was observed only after hours of interaction with P. aeruginosa.
source: However, the avoidance behavior was observed only after hours of interaction with P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited prior work.

claim: The activity of the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway is required to elicit the avoidance behavior.
source: Therefore, while the activity of the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway is required to elicit the avoidance behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), its rapid activation in ASJ neurons by chemosensation appears to be insufficient for induction of this behavior.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rapid activation of DAF-7/TGF-β in ASJ neurons by chemosensation appears to be insufficient for induction of avoidance behavior.
source: Therefore, while the activity of the DAF-7/TGF-β pathway is required to elicit the avoidance behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), its rapid activation in ASJ neurons by chemosensation appears to be insufficient for induction of this behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the timing mismatch between DAF-7 activation and avoidance behavior.

claim: The DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1/GPCR pathways are induced by intestinal bloating.
source: Because the DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1/GPCR pathways are induced by intestinal bloating (Singh and Aballay, 2019a) and act synergistically to elicit pathogen avoidance (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), it is likely that animals integrate multiple inputs, including intestinal infection and chemosensation, to induce defense responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1/GPCR pathways act synergistically to elicit pathogen avoidance.
source: Because the DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1/GPCR pathways are induced by intestinal bloating (Singh and Aballay, 2019a) and act synergistically to elicit pathogen avoidance (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), it is likely that animals integrate multiple inputs, including intestinal infection and chemosensation, to induce defense responses.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Animals integrate multiple inputs, including intestinal infection and chemosensation, to induce defense responses.
source: Because the DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1/GPCR pathways are induced by intestinal bloating (Singh and Aballay, 2019a) and act synergistically to elicit pathogen avoidance (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), it is likely that animals integrate multiple inputs, including intestinal infection and chemosensation, to induce defense responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that both chemosensation and bloating contribute to defense responses.

claim: In addition to O2, animals sense CO2 and NO from bacterial lawns via multiple chemosensory neurons to control the pathogen avoidance behavior.
source: Indeed, in addition to O2, animals sense CO2 and NO from bacterial lawns via multiple chemosensory neurons to control the pathogen avoidance behavior (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015; Hao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans possesses an innate attraction to the smell of P. aeruginosa.
source: C. elegans possesses an innate attraction to the smell of P. aeruginosa, and a brief exposure to P. aeruginosa does not lead to changes in preference to E. coli (Ha et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A brief exposure to P. aeruginosa does not lead to changes in preference to E. coli.
source: C. elegans possesses an innate attraction to the smell of P. aeruginosa, and a brief exposure to P. aeruginosa does not lead to changes in preference to E. coli (Ha et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The olfactory aversive learning of P. aeruginosa and changes in preference to E. coli require several hours of exposure to P. aeruginosa.
source: Because the olfactory aversive learning of P. aeruginosa and changes in preference to E. coli require several hours of exposure to P. aeruginosa, the mechanism by which the animals learn to avoid pathogens over time remain unclear.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited prior work.

claim: Bloating of the intestine caused by P. aeruginosa infection is required for the learning process.
source: Here we show that bloating of the intestine caused by P. aeruginosa infection is required for the learning process.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The learning involves modulation of aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal bloating.
source: We demonstrate that the learning involves modulation of aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways by intestinal bloating.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: By genetic modulation of the aerotaxis behavior of the animals, a rapid change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli can be induced.
source: By genetic modulation of the aerotaxis behavior of the animals, we are able to induce a rapid change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Feeding on several pathogenic, but not nonpathogenic, bacteria leads to colonization and bloating of the intestine.
source: Feeding on several pathogenic, but not nonpathogenic, bacteria leads to colonization and bloating of the intestine (Fuhrman et al., 2009; Irazoqui et al., 2010; Kurz et al., 2003; Yuen and Ausubel, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The bloating-induced defense response might be a generalized response of C. elegans to infection by different pathogens.
source: Thus, the bloating-induced defense response might be a generalized response of C. elegans to infection by different pathogens and enables the animals to distinguish between pathogenic and innocuous microbes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that multiple pathogens cause bloating.

claim: The bloating-induced defense response enables the animals to distinguish between pathogenic and innocuous microbes.
source: Thus, the bloating-induced defense response might be a generalized response of C. elegans to infection by different pathogens and enables the animals to distinguish between pathogenic and innocuous microbes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that bloating is specific to pathogenic bacteria.

claim: The induction of intestinal bloating by genetic manipulation activates avoidance behavior towards even nonpathogenic bacteria.
source: Indeed, the induction of intestinal bloating by genetic manipulation activates avoidance behavior towards even nonpathogenic bacteria (Kumar et al., 2019; Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The neuropeptide Y (NPY)-related signaling neuroendocrine pathway NPR-1 appears to have a conserved mode of activation and action across a variety of disparate species.
source: Interestingly, the neuropeptide Y (NPY)-related signaling neuroendocrine pathway NPR-1, which is activated by intestinal bloating in C. elegans, appears to have a conserved mode of activation and action across a variety of disparate species (Duvall et al., 2019; Singh and Aballay, 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gut distension caused by a complete blood meal may activate the NPY-related signaling in mosquitoes and induce host aversion.
source: For instance, gut distension caused by a complete blood meal may activate the NPY-related signaling in mosquitoes and induce host aversion (Singh and Aballay, 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: C. elegans possesses a rhythmic defecation cycle that is timed by an oscillation in intestinal pH.
source: C. elegans possesses a rhythmic defecation cycle that is timed by an oscillation in intestinal pH (Pfeiffer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Defects in the pH wave lead to defects in the defecation cycle causing intestinal bloating.
source: Defects in the pH wave lead to defects in the defecation cycle causing intestinal bloating (Pfeiffer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pathogenic bacteria such as P. aeruginosa and Enterococcus faecalis, but not nonpathogenic E. coli, disturb the pH wave in C. elegans intestine.
source: Pathogenic bacteria such as P. aeruginosa and Enterococcus faecalis, but not nonpathogenic E. coli, disturb the pH wave in C. elegans intestine (Benomar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is possible that disturbance of pH wave by pathogens leads to intestinal bloating in C. elegans.
source: It is possible that it is this disturbance of pH wave by pathogens that leads to intestinal bloating in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of bloating.

claim: C. elegans recognizes potential pathogen attack by sensing homeostasis perturbations, including perturbations of core cellular processes, DNA damage, and intestinal bloating.
source: Increasing evidence shows that C. elegans recognizes potential pathogen attack by sensing homeostasis perturbations, including perturbations of core cellular processes, DNA damage, and intestinal bloating (Dunbar et al., 2012; Ermolaeva et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2019; McEwan et al., 2012; Melo and Ruvkun, 2012; Pukkila-Worley, 2016; Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Physiological changes induced by pathogen infection or toxins generate modifications in C. elegans homeostasis that elicit an innate immune response and microbial aversion behavior via neuroendocrine signaling.
source: Thus, these studies show that the physiological changes induced by pathogen infection or toxins generate modifications in C. elegans homeostasis that elicit an innate immune response and microbial aversion behavior via neuroendocrine signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cited studies and the current manuscript's findings.

claim: C. elegans mounts immune responses toward heat-killed pathogenic bacteria.
source: C. elegans mounts immune responses toward heat-killed pathogenic bacteria (Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012; Yuen and Ausubel, 2018), suggesting the possible existence of MAMP-like mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heat-killed bacteria could lead to intestinal bloating and activation of defense responses.
source: However, the interpretation of these results is not straightforward because heat-killed bacteria could lead to intestinal bloating and activation of defense responses (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recent studies in Drosophila melanogaster highlight the role of intestinal infection in modulating the immune response and social behavior.
source: Recent studies in Drosophila melanogaster also highlight the role of intestinal infection in modulating the immune response and social behavior (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The modulation of behavior by intestinal infection appears to be conserved across species.
source: Therefore, the modulation of behavior by intestinal infection appears to be conserved across species.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in both C. elegans and Drosophila.
